Middle
MID-dl
adj. / n.
From Old English middel. Webster 1828: equally distant from the extremes; intervening; intermediate. The word’s great theological use is Paul’s middle wall of partition, the barrier in the temple court between Jew and Gentile, which he says Christ broke down.

Biblical Definition

Middle is fixed in Christian vocabulary by one phrase: he is our peace, who hath made both one, and hath broken down the middle wall of partition between us (Ephesians 2:14). The reference is almost certainly to the low stone barrier in the temple at Jerusalem which separated the court of the Gentiles from the inner courts, carrying inscriptions in Greek and Latin warning that any foreigner passing it had only himself to blame for his death. Paul, who had been accused of bringing a Greek past that wall and was nearly killed for it, writes from prison that Christ has demolished it. The chapter is exact about what was removed and how: the enmity, even the law of commandments contained in ordinances — the ceremonial partition of clean and unclean, circumcision and uncircumcision — abolished in his flesh, so as to make in Himself of twain one new man. The word appears elsewhere in ordinary senses: Samson took hold of the two middle pillars, and the veil of the temple was rent in the midst. But the middle wall is the one that decides how a church looks, because the two peoples were not reconciled by a compromise between them but by both being reconciled to God in one body by the cross.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines MIDDLE as equally distant from the extremes; intervening; intermediate; and as a noun, the point or part equally distant from the extremities. The 1828 entry is purely spatial; the theological weight comes from Ephesians 2:14.

expand to see more

MIDDLE, a. — Equally distant from the extremes; as the middle point of a line, the middle station of life.

Intervening; intermediate; occupying the place between others.

MIDDLE, n. — The point or part equally distant from the extremities.

Middle wall — a partition wall; the phrase of Ephesians 2:14, referring to the barrier of the temple court.

Josephus describes the temple balustrade and the inscriptions upon it forbidding Gentiles to pass, which is the background of Paul’s figure.

Key Scripture

Ephesians 2:14 — "For he is our peace, who hath made both one, and hath broken down the middle wall of partition between us;"

Ephesians 2:15 — "Having abolished in his flesh the enmity, even the law of commandments contained in ordinances; for to make in himself of twain one new man, so making peace;"

Ephesians 2:16 — "And that he might reconcile both unto God in one body by the cross, having slain the enmity thereby:"

Galatians 3:28 — "There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither bond nor free, there is neither male nor female: for ye are all one in Christ Jesus."

Colossians 2:14 — "Blotting out the handwriting of ordinances that was against us, which was contrary to us, and took it out of the way, nailing it to his cross;"

Modern Corruption

Ephesians 2 and Galatians 3:28 are the two most abused unity texts in the New Testament, pressed to abolish distinctions Scripture maintains elsewhere — particularly the creational distinction of male and female and the ordered offices of the church.

expand to see more

Paul names exactly what was broken down: the enmity, even the law of commandments contained in ordinances — the ceremonial system that fenced Israel from the nations. That partition is gone, and any church that rebuilds it in another form, whether by ethnic preference or by cultural gatekeeping, is re-erecting what Christ demolished. What Paul does not say is that all distinctions whatever have been dissolved. In the same letter he addresses husbands and wives, parents and children, masters and servants, each in their own order, and he does it three chapters later. Galatians 3:28 is a statement about standing before God in justification — ye are all one in Christ Jesus, all Abraham’s seed, all heirs — not a denial that God made them male and female.

The egalitarian argument that Galatians 3:28 abolishes the created order proves far too much, since the same verse names bond and free, and no one supposes Paul meant that the household codes of Ephesians 6 were thereby cancelled — he wrote them afterward. The apostle who penned neither male nor female also penned 1 Timothy 2:12-13 and grounded it in the order of creation, not in culture. The right reading holds both: identical standing before God, and ordered relations within the household and the church. That is not a tension to be managed; it is the same structure the Trinity itself exhibits, equality of essence with order of relation.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek mesotoichon (G3320), a middle wall, joined with phragmos (G5418), a fence or partition, at Ephesians 2:14; mesos (G3319), middle.

expand to see more

Greek mesotoichon (G3320) — a middle wall; a hapax legomenon at Ephesians 2:14.

Greek phragmos (G5418) — a fence, hedge, partition; joined to the previous word in the same phrase.

Greek mesos (G3319) — middle, midst; the common adjective.

Greek echthra (G2189) — enmity, hostility; what the wall embodied and Christ slew (Ephesians 2:16).

Greek dogma (G1378) — a decree, ordinance; the law of commandments contained in ordinances (Ephesians 2:15).

Usage

"Hath broken down the middle wall of partition (Ephesians 2:14) — the temple barrier demolished in Christ’s flesh."

"To make in himself of twain one new man (Ephesians 2:15) — not a compromise but a new creation."

"Reconcile both unto God in one body by the cross (Ephesians 2:16) — peace with each other through peace with God."
